newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's IFP seeks pensions for apartheid fight.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's IFP seeks pensions for apartheid fight.

text.p: South Africa's conservative Inkatha Freedom Party sought on Tuesday to win special pensions for members who opposed apartheid but the rival African National Congress said they did not qualify.

IFP legislator Gavin Woods complained during a meeting of parliament's powerful finance committee about provisions in the Special Pensions Bill that excluded Inkatha members because the party had never been banned.

The bill proposes modest pensions of up to 42,000 rand ($9,275) a year for former permanent staff of outlawed political movements such as the ANC, the Pan Africanist Congress and the South African Communist Party.
Woods said allies of Zulu Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi's fight against white rule should be treated in the same way as veterans of President Nelson Mandela's ANC.
"The IFP is concerned about fairness. It is a very topical issue within the party," Woods told the multi-party committee.
He said that though the IFP was never banned, its members suffered more than ANC members because it did not have the foreign support given to the ANC in exile.
ANC member Barbara Hogan said Mandela's party, which dominates the committee, would oppose the IFP's request for inclusion "with regret".
She said the draft law was intended to help those who had not been able to accumulate pension rights due to their organisations having been banned.

"This is not a struggle pension, much as we wish it was. It is a compensation for people who were marginalised under apartheid and prevented from earning a pension," she told reporters after the meeting.
Woods told reporters that the IFP would oppose the bill when parliament votes on it later this year.

"Part of the animosity between ourselves and the ANC has been because they refuse to recognise the IFP as a bona fide liberation movement, which made a significant contribution to the fight against apartheid," he said.
The ANC and the IFP have been locked in a bitter political turf war in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province since the mid-1980s.

Hogan said the government estimated that up to 22,000 people might qualify for a pension, which would be payable from the age of 60. She said any attempt to extend the scheme to people who fought apartheid legally would cost far too much.
